Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Vignette:
Michael, a 49-year-old city council member, sat in his office on a bright Tuesday morning, the sunlight streaming through the large windows. Yet, despite the beautiful day outside, an oppressive weight settled on his chest. Michael had always believed that the world was a place of opportunity and promise, but since returning from combat service overseas, he felt suffocated by an undercurrent of danger. It was as if a dark cloud loomed over him, distorting his perception of reality. He was married and had two grown children, yet the warmth of family gatherings felt muted, overshadowed by a persistent sense of dread.

The memories of his time in combat haunted him relentlessly. He often found himself grasping at fragmented recollections of the events that unfolded during his deployment. There were flashes of explosions, the sounds of gunfire, and the faces of comrades who had fought bravely alongside him, but the details remained elusive, like wisps of smoke that slipped through his fingers. When he attempted to recount his experiences to anyone, the words would falter, and he would lose the thread of his own narrative, leaving him feeling helpless and frustrated.

Over time, Michael's coping mechanisms morphed into maladaptive strategies. Loud music or the blaring of the television became his refuge, drowning out intrusive memories and thoughts. Yet, those distractions only provided temporary relief. He instinctively monitored his own thoughts, fearful that any slip might lead him down a path of madness. Each time he felt a flicker of anxiety, he would quickly shift his focus to something—anything—to quell the rising tide of panic.

Physical contact became a source of great distress for him. It started with a jolt of alarm whenever someone brushed against him unexpectedly—an instinctive reaction that betrayed how deeply he had internalized the threat of danger. He would flinch at the slightest touch, no matter how innocent, and this instinctive avoidance extended to his family. The warmth of a hug from his wife, which once brought comfort, now felt like a reminder of the chaos he had endured in combat. He would stiffen and pull away, convincing himself that it was safer to remain untouched, his body perceiving danger where none existed.

Sleep, too, eluded him. Michael would lie awake at night, his mind racing. Thoughts of his brothers-in-arms, some of whom had not returned, plagued him. He would toss and turn, unable to find solace, convinced that sleep would leave him vulnerable. In those dark hours, he would often recall the terror of his experiences in the field, memories that surged back with vivid clarity, bringing with them the same visceral fear he had felt in those moments of life and death.

The world outside his office felt increasingly menacing. Even in the bustling city, surrounded by colleagues and constituents, he couldn’t shake the feeling that danger lurked just beneath the surface. He found himself hypervigilant, scanning his environment for potential threats, convinced that he had to remain on guard at all times. This pervasive sense of mistrust in his surroundings made it impossible for him to feel safe, even when others reassured him that he was in a secure space.

Michael's growing isolation took a toll on his relationships. His wife, once his closest confidante, now looked at him with concern, struggling to bridge the chasm that had formed between them. Their conversations became strained, with Michael often withdrawing into silence, feeling as though he was a stranger in his own home. He wanted to reach out, to connect, but the fear of his own reactions held him back. 

In recent weeks, a particularly vivid memory of combat had surfaced, sending him spiraling into a renewed state of distress. The terror of that recollection drove him to the brink, and he realized he could no longer navigate this turmoil alone. It was a moment of clarity amidst the chaos; a whispered urge to seek help emerged from the shadows of his mind. As he sat in his office, surrounded by the familiar trappings of his life, he felt a flicker of hope. Perhaps reaching out for support could bring him back to a place of safety—the safety he yearned for but had struggled to believe existed.
